# Psalm 46 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Title and Superscription

**"For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song."**

- The sons of Korah were Levites from the family of Kohath who served in the musical aspect of temple worship (2 Chronicles 20:19). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Alamoth**: The Hebrew *'alāmôth* means "maidens"; the most natural and now generally received interpretation is "a song for sopranos" (a musical direction). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- Adam Clarke suggested it could mean "a choir of singing girls." Spurgeon wondered if it referred to a high-pitched stringed instrument (per 1 Chronicles 15:20). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Historical setting**: Most commentators connect this psalm with the destruction of Sennacherib's army in the time of Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:35). Delitzsch adopts Jehoshaphat's deliverance (2 Chronicles 20) as an alternative. The psalm has remarkable parallels with Isaiah (e.g., the expression "God is with us" echoes Immanuel). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-46.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm

---

## v. 1 — "God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble."

- **Traditional reading**: The psalm unusually opens with God's provision rather than the psalmist's crisis. The poet speaks from experience: God Himself is a place of refuge (like the cities of refuge in Israel), God Himself is strength for His people, and God alone (not God plus something else) is their help. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Ellicott**: "Refuge and strength" is better rendered "a refuge and stronghold, or a sure stronghold," as in Luther's hymn *Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott*. "A very present help" is better "often found a help." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Pulpit**: "A very present Help" = literally "a very accessible Help — one easy to be found" (cf. 2 Chronicles 15:4). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: The verb "he is found" is in the past tense, indicating God has been proven a help in past tribulations. Calvin stresses that this applies to God's covenant people specifically — God "exercises a special care in preserving and defending her." The promise is for all times but for the people of God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)**: "We may be as timid by nature as the coneys, but God is our refuge; we are as weak by nature as bruised reeds, but God is our strength." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **G. Campbell Morgan**: "The secret of the confidence is the consciousness of the nearness of God." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

---

## v. 2 — "Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas"

- **Traditional reading**: The psalmist applies "the logic of faith" — if God is truly refuge, strength, and help, there is no logical reason to fear, even in the biggest crisis. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Ellicott**: "Though the earth be removed" = literally "at the changing of the earth," possibly with the figure of a worn-out garment (Psalm 102:26). The psalmist is thinking of earthquake convulsions and figures Israel fearless amid tottering kingdoms and falling dynasties. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Pulpit**: The "mountains carried into the midst of the sea" is a metaphor for violent political disturbances — probably those caused by the Assyrian career of conquest under Sennacherib. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: These are "hyperbolical modes of expression" denoting a revolution and turning upside down of the whole world. Calvin stresses that "we will not fear" does not mean believers are exempt from all emotion — "there is a great difference between insensibility and the confidence of faith." Believers are never overwhelmed with terror but gather strength to allay all fear. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Kidner**: "Its robust, defiant tone suggests that it was composed at a time of crisis, which makes the confession of faith doubly impressive." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

---

## v. 3 — "though their waters roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge. Selah"

- **Ellicott**: The original Hebrew is very expressive in its conciseness: "They roar, they foam, its waters." Compares to Homer's concise description of ocean (Iliad xxiii. 230). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Pulpit**: The waters "roar and foam" (Hengstenberg, Kay, Cheyne); the imagery depicts the raging of nations as roaring seas (cf. Psalm 93:3-4). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Selah**: A pause for reflection. Spurgeon remarked, "It were well if all of us could say, 'Selah,' under tempestuous trials, but alas! too often we speak in our haste, lay our trembling hands bewildered among the strings, strike the lyre with a rude crash, and mar the melody of our life-song." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Expositor's Bible Commentary**: The refrain ("The LORD of hosts is with us…") probably originally appeared after v. 3 but has dropped out of the text. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-46.html

---

## v. 4 — "There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells."

- **Traditional reading**: The scene shifts dramatically from roaring, chaotic seas to a quiet, life-giving river. Jerusalem in reality has no great river — only a few small streams (like the brook Kidron or Siloam). The river is therefore a symbol of God's peaceful, abundant, constant provision and presence. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Ellicott**: The Hebrew *nāhar* means a perennial stream (as distinct from *nāchal*, a dry torrent bed). The Kidron is not alluded to; many commentators think Siloam is intended. Or there may be no local allusion — the river is simply a symbol of the peace and blessing of the Divine presence, as the sea in vv. 2-3 symbolizes the world's noisy troubles. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Pulpit**: The "river" imagery points to "the perennial fountain of God's grace — that 'pure river of water of life,' which, welling forth from the throne of God and of the Lamb, continually refreshes and gladdens the Church of Christ" (Revelation 22:1). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: Calvin sees a deliberate contrast: those who seek earthly defenses imagine they are protected as if surrounded by a sea, but God's people are satisfied with "a gently flowing stream." He connects this to Isaiah 8:6 where the Jews are rebuked for despising "the gently flowing waters of Shiloah" and longing for the deep, rapid rivers of Assyria and Egypt. Even though God's help comes "in a secret and gentle manner, like the still flowing streams, yet it imparts to us more tranquillity of mind than if the whole power of the world were gathered together for our help." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Maclaren**: "We might almost translate, 'Lo! a river!' Jerusalem was unique among historical cities in that it had no great river. It had one tiny thread of water." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Prophetic connection**: The prophets anticipated a mighty river flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47:12; Revelation 22:1). This future reality is already in the psalmist's mind. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Kidner**: "With God the waters are no longer menacing seas but a life-giving river." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

---

## v. 5 — "God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns."

- **Traditional reading**: The city's stability comes not from walls or geography but from God's indwelling presence. Because of His presence, the city is more firmly set than the earth which may be moved (v. 2). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: "While the world is being turned upside down (vv. 2, 3, 6), the Church is unmoved — since 'God is in the midst of her.'" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **"When morning dawns" / "right early"**: Literally "at the turning of the morning." The Pulpit Commentary connects this specifically to the deliverance from Sennacherib: it was discovered "early in the morning" that 185,000 Assyrians were dead corpses (2 Kings 19:35). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Ellicott**: The phrase is "evidently metaphorical of the dawn of a brighter day." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: The expression denotes that God will come daily, "as soon as the sun rises upon the earth." God does not always hasten immediately to our aid according to our desires, but He comes seasonably. Calvin emphasizes: "If we desire to be protected by the hand of God, we must be concerned above all things that he may dwell amongst us; for all hope of safety depends upon his presence alone." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm

---

## v. 6 — "Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice."

- **Traditional reading**: As in Psalm 2, God pays no regard to the rage of the nations. At His mere voice the earth melts away — a striking contrast between noisy human rebellion and the effortless power of God's word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: The past tenses are probably "the preterite of prophetic certainty" — the writer foresees and announces the destruction of Israel's enemies as though it has already happened. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Ellicott**: The absence of conjunctions and sudden change from preterite to future lends vividness: "Raged heathen, tottered kingdoms / Gave with His voice (the signal) (and lo!) / Melts the earth." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: This verse confirms "from experience the doctrine which he had advanced concerning the impregnable character of the divine protection." It teaches that "although the whole world rise up against us, and confound all things by their increased madness, they can be brought to nought in a moment, as soon as God shows himself favourable towards us." The "voice of God" signifies His will or command — Calvin sees an allusion to the promises of God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm

---

## v. 7 — "The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah"

- **Traditional reading**: This is the confident chorus/refrain of the psalm (repeated in v. 11). The two divine titles present God in two aspects: (1) **Yahweh Sabaoth / LORD of Hosts** — the cosmic King, commander of all armies of heaven and earth; (2) **God of Jacob** — the personal, covenant God who bound Himself to a rather unworthy patriarch, emphasizing grace. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: "The Lord of hosts" means God "has countless angels at his command" (2 Kings 6:16-17; Psalm 68:17; Matthew 26:53). "The God of Jacob" emphasizes the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Ellicott**: "Refuge" here (different Hebrew word from v. 1) carries the "idea of height, as giving security" — an inaccessible high stronghold. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: This verse teaches that we can only apply God's power to ourselves when "we believe ourselves to be of the number of those whom God has embraced with his fatherly love." Faith must consider both God's "immeasurable power" and "his fatherly love which he has manifested in his word." Calvin warns that those who interpret Scripture while leaving in suspense the application of God's power to themselves "err egregiously." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Maclaren**: "When we say 'The God of Jacob,' we reach back into the past and lay hold of the Helper of the men of old as ours." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

---

## v. 8 — "Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth."

- **Traditional reading**: The emphasis shifts from God as refuge and help to a consideration of God's glory demonstrated in His mighty works. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Ellicott**: "Desolations" — the primary sense of the Hebrew word is "silence of desolation," or (as in Jeremiah 19:8) "wonders, which silence by their suddenness and marvel." The LXX and Vulgate take this sense, confirmed by v. 10. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Pulpit**: The deliverance of Israel is effected by "desolations" or "devastations" which God accomplishes among the nations. The announcement is "very vague and general," applicable to almost any occasion when God's people were delivered from pressing peril. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: Calvin sees this as a rebuke to human indifference: "there is scarcely one in a hundred who acknowledges that he has abundant help and security in God, so that they are all blinded to the works of God, or rather wilfully shut their eyes." He calls all to "consider the works of God" because people ascribe to fortune or their own industry what God alone has done. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm

---

## v. 9 — "He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire."

- **Traditional reading**: God's people are invited to look over the field of battle after God has completely routed His enemies. Their instruments of war are scattered, broken, and burning. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: Each great deliverance is followed by a term of peace (Judges 3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28), each typical of the final peace when God puts all enemies under Messiah's feet (Isaiah 2:4; 11:9; 65:25). War-chariots were the main strength of Sennacherib's army (2 Kings 19:23). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Expositor's Bible Commentary**: The language "is naturally applied to the relics of Sennacherib's annihilated force… Broken bows, splintered spears, half-charred chariots, strew the ground, and Israel can go forth without fear and feast their eyes on these tokens of what God has done." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-46.html
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: God is "set forth as adorned with these titles, that we should look for peace from him, even when the whole world is in uproar, and agitated in a dreadful manner." Calvin notes there was an ancient custom of collecting arms of the vanquished into a heap and setting them on fire (cf. Joshua 11:6; Ezekiel 39:8-10), symbolizing complete victory. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm

---

## v. 10 — "Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth."

- **Traditional reading (majority view)**: This is God Himself speaking. The command "Be still" is not primarily comfort for the weary believer (though it is often applied that way devotionally). In context, it is a rebuke to the restless, warring nations: "Lay down your arms. Surrender, and acknowledge that I am the one and only victorious God" (Boice). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Kidner**: "Be still…is not in the first place comfort for the harassed but a rebuke to a restless and turbulent world: 'Quiet!' — in fact, 'Leave off!'" — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: "As a general rule, God requires man to cooperate with him… But there are occasions when man must stand aloof, and all must be left to the almighty Disposer of all things. The invasion of Sennacherib was such an occasion. Human effort could not but be futile." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **Ellicott**: "The introduction of the Divine Protector Himself speaking just before the refrain is a fine touch of art." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)**: Calvin understands this as addressed specifically to the enemies of God's people: "in doing injury to the saints they do not consider that they are making war against God." God bids them "be still and hold their peace, so that when their anger is appeased they may perceive that they are fighting against God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Expositor's Bible Commentary**: "Desist" (or "Be still") = literally "Let your hands drop" — i.e., "Ground your weapons." God desires that foes "would cease their vain strife before it proves fatal." The prospect of a world submissive to its King "softens the terrors of His destructive manifestations, reveals their inmost purpose, and opens to foes the possibility of passing, not as conquerors, but as subjects…through the gate into the city." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-46.html
- **Horne**: "In this verse there is a change of person, and Jehovah himself is introduced, as commanding the world to cease its opposition, to own his power, and to acknowledge his sovereignty over all the kingdoms of the nations." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Jonathan Edwards** (Reformed): "Our submission is to be such as becomes rational creatures. God doth not require us to submit contrary to reason, but to submit as seeing the reason and ground of submission. Hence, the bare consideration that God is God may well be sufficient to still all objections and oppositions against the divine sovereign." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

---

## v. 11 — "The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah"

- **Traditional reading**: The refrain repeats, closing the psalm with confidence and serenity. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Pulpit**: Same as v. 7 — "The Lord of hosts is with us" is the ground of assurance; "The God of Jacob" is the covenant-keeping God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/46.htm
- **John Wesley (Methodist)**: On his deathbed, Wesley had nearly lost his voice but suddenly called out, "The best of all is, God is with us." Then, raising his hand and waving it in triumph, he exclaimed again, "The best of all is, God is with us." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

## Cross-Tradition Distinctives

### Lutheran
- **Martin Luther** drew such strength from this psalm that in his darkest distress he would say, "Let us sing the forty-sixth psalm in concert; and then let the devil do his worst." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/ (citing John Trapp)
- Luther composed his famous hymn *"Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott"* ("A Mighty Fortress Is Our God") as a paraphrase of Psalm 46, on his journey to the Diet of Worms where he defended the Reformation at the risk of his life. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm (footnote)
- The phrase "a sure stronghold" in Ellicott is directly connected to Luther's translation: *"Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott."* — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm

### Reformed (distinctive emphases)
- **Calvin** emphasizes that the protections described are for God's *covenant people specifically*, not all humanity generally. The psalm draws "a distinction between the chosen people of God and other heathen nations." Faith must combine both God's power and His fatherly covenant love, or else "the description of the power of God would only inspire us with dread." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/46.htm
- **Calvin on v. 4**: God's help comes "in a secret and gentle manner, like the still flowing streams," not through worldly power and show. This is a distinctly Reformed emphasis on God working through humble, apparently weak means.
- **Jonathan Edwards** (on v. 10): The command to "be still" is a call to rational submission — "the bare consideration that God is God may well be sufficient to still all objections." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

### Baptist
- **Charles Spurgeon** ("Treasury of David") is cited extensively throughout the Enduring Word commentary. His emphases: (a) the contrast between natural human weakness and God's strength (v. 1); (b) the importance of *Selah* — pausing under trial rather than speaking in haste (v. 3); (c) God as the refuge of the individual soul.

### Methodist/Wesleyan
- **John Wesley's** deathbed words (on v. 11): "The best of all is, God is with us" — emphasizing personal experience and assurance. — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Adam Clarke** (Methodist): Suggested Alamoth could refer to "a choir of singing girls." On v. 5, "As by the day-break the shadows and darkness are dissipated; so by the bright rising of Jehovah, the darkness of adversity shall be scattered." — cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- Emphasis on *experiencing* God as refuge and strength ("He could say these things by experience"), the personal nearness of God (citing Morgan), and the Holy Spirit's application of the psalm to the individual believer's trials. Guzik also highlights the forward-looking prophetic dimension — the river pointing toward Ezekiel 47 and the New Jerusalem, and the ultimate exaltation of God among all nations.

### Anglican
- **Ellicott** focuses on careful translation, the poetic structure (three strophes, refrain), and historical context (7th century BC, Assyrian crisis). Notes the literary quality: the "fine touch of art" when God Himself speaks in v. 10. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/46.htm

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching
- The devotional misreading of v. 10 ("Be still and know that I am God" as a call to personal quiet time/contemplation) is explicitly corrected by several commentators. **Boice** states it "is not advice to us to lead a contemplative life, however important that may be… It means rather, 'Lay down your arms. Surrender, and acknowledge that I am the one and only victorious God.'" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-46/
- **Kidner** likewise insists it is "not in the first place comfort for the harassed but a rebuke to a restless and turbulent world." — cited in same source.
- The **Expositor's Bible Commentary** bridges the two: the command is to foes to "ground your weapons," yet it also "softens the terrors" and opens the possibility of entering the city as subjects rather than conquerors. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-46.html
